items.summary: CargoWise users handling British and Japanese customs declarations suffered messaging delays on Wednesday, while the backlog had been fully cleared the following morning. Customer notifications seen by The Loadstar show WiseTech acknowledged an issue affecting message responses at 10.37am on 28 October. At 11.24, it confirmed that GB and Japan customs messaging were “particularly impacted”. One UK forwarder said the disruption prevented its team from processing customs entries normally for much of the working day, leaving customers waiting and staff struggling to provide useful information. Subsequent updates at 12.04 and 14.07pm said engineers were working on mitigation, before a 3.51pm notice reported backlogs ‘processing slowly’. At 8.47pm, the company said the backlog across most queues had been processed, but teams remained ‘engaged on the core issue’ and working towards full restoration. At 8.33am yesterday, it confirmed that the backlog had been fully processed, and messaging services had recovered. The notifications span almost 22 hours, between acknowledgement and recovery confirmation, although they do not establish how long individual customers had been affected. The disruption follows a separate CargoWise outage reported by The Loadstar in June, when customers in several countries experienced log-in failures and electronic messaging problems.

However, the impact of such action would extend well beyond the security workforce. The threat comes as the South California port complex is handling record volumes. LA/LB processed an average of 68,000 teu a day in September, according to Mr Jensen, meaning even a short strike could quickly create bottlenecks for landside trucking and arriving vessels. CargoTrans reported that, on Monday, approximately 35,700 containers were awaiting rail transportation, including around 10,500 that had been at terminals for nine days or longer. And further logistical challenges are approaching: the Vincent Thomas Bridge is scheduled to close from 7 November for approximately 16 months, potentially lengthening drayage journeys through the port complex. items.title: How a New “Arab Dark Fleet” Keeps Hormuz Oil Flowing
items.original_title: How a New “Arab Dark Fleet” Keeps Hormuz Oil Flowing
items.summary: Gulf oil producers have gained control of a fleet of nearly 230 tankers that have defied Iran to ship oil through the Strait of Hormuz and keep the chokepoint open to global trade. The giant fleet is owned, managed, chartered or controlled by Gulf national oil companies or their trading and shipping arms and is designed to cut reliance on chartering tankers on the spot market. Despite very high freight rates, fewer shipowners will send tankers to load at oil terminals in Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman or the UAE. The result is a new fleet, the Arab Dark Fleet, solely deployed by Gulf states and dedicated to keeping their oil flowing. The “Arab Dark Fleet” is the biggest shift in how Gulf national oil companies run their freight, logistics, and supply chains since the Tanker War of the 1980s. The South Korean shipowner began buying and chartering VLCCs in December 2025 and has built a fleet of more than 100 ships, about 70% of which now work in the Arab Dark Fleet. items.title: Shifts in cement trade help support the Supramax market
items.original_title: Shifts in cement trade help support the Supramax market
items.summary: China’s property slump has turned Asia’s cement trade inside out. Its exports are a mix of roughly 60% cement and 40% clinker, and this year the average cargo looks set to travel about three times as far as it did in 2019. These are Supramax-sized parcels on some of the longest routes in the trade, and the new 50% tariff on Canadian cement may stretch them further. They are shipping about a quarter more cement than in 2019, but the tonne-miles have doubled. So every million tonnes that moves from the short route to a long one ties up around four more ships for a year, and across the trade the extra distance since 2019 is worth the full-time work of around 110 Supramaxes in 2026. Because the long hauls go on the bigger ships, Supramax tonne-miles in cement from China and Vietnam look set to rise by more than 80% this year, against about a third for Handysizes. Support for the Supramax market So what does it add up to? When a fleet is close to fully employed, small changes in demand can have an outsized effect on rates, so the extra miles look supportive for Supramax earnings through 2026. The support fades in 2027 as hauls shorten, then levels out in 2028.

items.title: Same Trade Lane, Different Footprint: Carrier Emissions Intensity Differs by Up to 35% on Major Container Routes
items.original_title: Same Trade Lane, Different Footprint: Carrier Emissions Intensity Differs by Up to 35% on Major Container Routes
items.summary: The report also shows why absolute emissions are a poor measure of efficiency. On the China/East Asia–Northern Europe trade, the carrier with the lowest emissions intensity, out of the three carriers examined, also recorded the highest average emissions per voyage, highlighting the importance of cargo volumes and vessel utilization when assessing environmental performance. Based on an analysis of 83,817 voyages performed by 6,730 container-carrying vessels, the report examines how actual vessel operations, including sailing patterns, port stays, cargo utilization and vessel deployment, influence maritime emissions performance. On the Northern Europe–North America East Coast trade, port time jumped 52.1% to 2.1 days. On direct China/East Asia–Northern Europe voyages, Evergreen recorded the highest average emissions of the three carriers examined (14,273 tonnes CO₂e), yet achieved the lowest intensity, at 47.4 g CO₂e/TEU-km, about 17% below the trade average of 57.3. At the same time, NeoPanamax and VLCS made up just 7% of voyages but generated 43% of transport work. This approach enables the company to examine performance across vessels, carriers, routes and operational conditions, rather than relying exclusively on published emission factors or aggregate carrier data. While industry, trade and carrier averages help identify trends, shipment-specific execution data and fuel-consumption modeling provide a more granular basis for understanding transportation performance and identifying opportunities to improve efficiency.

items.title: The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture
items.original_title: The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture
items.summary: Whatever the IMO decides in December, a broker will price a dry bulk trip the next morning. The vote changes which line of that fixture carries the carbon, and how much. The framework was approved in April 2025 and its adoption adjourned for a year last October; it was debated again at MEPC 84 in the spring. From 2028 every tonne of fuel burned on international voyages counts, wherever the ship trades, against two targets: a ship pays $100 for each tonne of CO2-equivalent between the direct-compliance line and the base line, and $380 for each tonne above the base line. On the Rotterdam trip, assuming no change to the European rules, that adds roughly €29,000 in 2028, taking the carbon on the fixture to about €96,000, or €1.45 a tonne and 12% of the hire. For the broker, the practical point is less the price of a tonne of carbon than its allocation. If the framework is adopted, every fixture acquires a carbon line, not only those touching Europe, and the charter party has to say who carries it. On a time-charter trip, the BIMCO clauses written for the EU ETS and FuelEU do not by themselves cover an IMO remedial unit.

items.original_title: Drone-hit boxship sinks off Bulgaria
items.summary: The Greek-managed containership Contship Jet has sunk off Bulgaria after being struck by three sea drones yesterday, as Russia claims further attacks on merchant vessels heading towards Ukrainian ports. The Liberian-flagged vessel, operated by Contships Management, was sailing from Haifa to Constanta when it was attacked approximately 17 nautical miles east of Cape Kaliakra. All 18 crew members, comprising 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians, were rescued by Bulgarian naval and border police vessels and taken to Varna. At least 20 containers fell overboard, prompting navigational warnings. This morning Moscow announced another attack on a general cargoship bound for Odesa, claiming the vessel was transporting military and dual-use equipment. Neither attack has been independently verified, and Russia has provided no vessel identities. The escalating maritime attacks prompted Turkish defence minister Yasar Guler to warn both Russia and Ukraine against targeting commercial shipping during security talks with his Bulgarian and Romanian counterparts yesterday. The three NATO members condemned the attacks and agreed to strengthen maritime intelligence sharing and early-warning arrangements. The latest incidents follow a succession of deadly strikes against merchant shipping off Romania and Bulgaria this month, including the October 23 sinking of Khoryv near Constanta, which left one seafarer dead and three missing.

items.title: Where are all the crew needed going to come from?
items.original_title: Where are all the crew needed going to come from?
items.summary: Shipping has never been short of ambition. The orderbook proves it. But increasingly, the industry again needs to ask itself the uncomfortable question: where are all the crew coming from? Today the physical risks are becoming impossible to ignore. My advice is simple: either manage your crew yourself, or go to where professional crew management is genuinely practised and get involved. The crew should feel that they belong to the owner, not merely to a management company. All too often, supposedly dedicated crew are taken from one owner’s pool and deployed to another owner’s vessel(s) when the manager has an urgent requirement — particularly where immediate matrix or tanker-compliance requirements need to be satisfied. There is simply no manager existing today of the scale and with the reserves of quality crew to take over management of say a large fleet of tankers without taking existing crew from other dedicated pools. Because the next generation of ships may be built of steel, composites, software and sophisticated technology, but without the right people on board, they are simply very expensive assets sitting idle in the water or trading dangerously and unsafely.

items.summary: Italian terminal operator Contship is getting back into the liner business, sealing a deal to acquire Italian shipping and logistics group Tarros through its subsidiary Sogemar, in a deal aimed at creating a major integrated transport network across the Mediterranean. The transaction covers the entire Tarros group, including its shipping operations, port handling businesses and inland logistics activities. Financial terms have not been disclosed. Founded in 1828, Tarros operates a door-to-door network spanning 16 countries and 31 ports, connecting European markets with North Africa and other Mediterranean destinations. The group employs 751 people and serves approximately 2,700 customers. The acquisition includes Tarros SpA and its overseas subsidiaries, Terminal del Golfo, Car Box, Compagnia Marittima Servizi and Med Logistics Malta. Contship intends to combine Tarros’s regional shipping services with Sogemar’s intermodal network and its existing terminal operations in Italy, Egypt and Morocco. The deal represents a significant consolidation of Mediterranean shortsea shipping and logistics operations, bringing together complementary maritime, terminal and inland transport networks. The acquisition remains subject to regulatory approvals, with completion expected during the fourth quarter of 2026.

items.summary: A CMA CGM containerships waits at anchor outside the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach have identified liquefied natural gas (LNG) and methanol as the most viable alternative marine fuels for the near and medium term, with a new study outlining potential demand and the infrastructure needed to support cleaner shipping at the nation’s busiest port complex. The joint Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , conducted as part of the ports’ Green Shipping Corridor initiatives, examined which alternative fuels shipping companies are most likely to adopt, how demand could develop through 2030, and what investments would be needed to support bunkering operations. The study estimates that annual LNG demand at the San Pedro Bay ports could reach between 65,000 and 115,000 metric tons by 2030, while methanol demand could range from 64,000 to 250,000 metric tons, depending on market conditions and the deployment of alternative-fuel vessels. The report also acknowledges that the environmental benefits of alternative marine fuels depend heavily on how they are produced and sourced. In April, the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach renewed their Green and Digital Shipping Corridor agreement with Singapore, with the partners committing to advance alternative-fuel bunkering, demonstration projects and digital connectivity.

Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other’s ports and vessels since the new grain marketing season started in July, bringing the once booming Black Sea agriculture trade to a standstill. “At a time when traditional export routes are facing restrictions, Murmansk Commercial Seaport is swiftly opening up an alternative route to foreign markets for Russian farmers,” the port said. Russia has rerouted its trade mostly to the Baltic Sea ports, which handled 1.2 million tons in September, accounting for over 60% of all seaborne grain exports. Turkey, an importer of grain from Russia, led the effort to introduce a ceasefire and resume shipments in the Black Sea, but Russia said it is no longer interested in a new Black Sea grain deal.

items.title: Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system
items.original_title: Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system
items.summary: A Norwegian-led consortium involving shipbuilder Vard and offshore vessel owner Island Offshore is preparing to build and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system, targeting its first vessel deployment in 2031 or 2032. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, will move from engineering studies to physical integration and testing, with a full-scale test facility planned at Stette near Ålesund in 2027. The project will combine Emerald Nuclear’s 5 MW electric Gem microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems. The initial testing phase will use electric heating instead of nuclear fuel to simulate reactor operation, allowing engineers to assess how the propulsion system performs under realistic vessel operating conditions. Tests will examine normal operation, rapid changes in power demand, system stress, emergency responses and interaction with ship crews. The consortium includes Vard Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Imperial College London and engineering specialist Maskindynamikk. The initiative builds on the NTNU-led NuProShip research programme, which has been examining the feasibility of integrating advanced nuclear reactors into commercial shipping. The latest pilot has received NOK20m ($2m) from the Research Council of Norway, while its initial development stage is expected to cost approximately NOK150m ($15.6m), including partner contributions.

items.original_title: Maritime CEO Forum: Shipping’s wartime boom tests discipline
items.summary: Shipping may be enjoying one of its strongest booms in decades, but the extraordinary profits generated by geopolitical turmoil are raising difficult questions about risk, investment and what happens when the wars end, delegates at yesterday’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco heard. Opening the event at the Yacht Club de Monaco, Splash editor Sam Chambers asked whether today’s riches were encouraging owners to repeat the mistakes of past cycles. Burak Cetinok, head of research at Arrow, described the rally as unusually broad across freight, vessel values and sale-and-purchase activity. His biggest concern was fresh capacity: Arrow’s analysis suggested that once an orderbook reaches roughly 25% of the existing fleet, earnings have historically tended to fall within 24 to 36 months. By the end of 2029, he said, almost half the fleet would be over 15 years old and a quarter over 20, creating considerable replacement demand. With tanker owners generally carrying much less debt than before the 2008 crash, he argued, the industry was also more resilient. Illustrating the desperation to secure oil supplies, Harfjeld described a refinery customer accepting a voyage 40 days longer, at a 50% higher freight rate, to avoid heightened Red Sea risks. According to the NTSB investigation report, the uncrewed vessel’s low-profile design made it particularly difficult for other mariners to see. The agency also issued three recommendations to NOAA, calling for revisions to its internal operating procedures to ensure its uncrewed vessels can be adequately detected by other mariners. items.title: Tariff anouncements cause cargo chaos for box terminals, says TiL
items.original_title: Tariff anouncements cause cargo chaos for box terminals, says TiL
items.summary: Sudden tariff announcements, not tariff levels themselves, trigger costly cargo surges that terminals cannot absorb, delegates at TOC Americas in Cartagena were told. Rather than destroying container trade, said TiL Group’s director for terminal investments in North America, Tom van Eynde, tariffs were relocating it, pointing to cargo shifting from Canadian ports into TiL’s US terminals as evidence. “It has been somewhat of a wild ride over the past year, the past two years,” Mr van Eynde noted, referring to tariffs in the US being introduced and then cancelled. “They’re not really reducing the trade flows, they’re just relocating them.” While the terminal operator saw a reduction in certain trade flows to the US through Canadian ports, he said these were then automatically being picked up by TiL terminals in US ports. Expecting the situation to be “a temporary thing”, Mr van Eynde said he expected disruption to settle once tariffs hit a range of 10% to 15% – “at that kind of level we see very little impact anymore on the volume.” The real damage, he said, came less from the tariffs themselves than from sudden announcements that triggered a rush of cargo before a deadline, only for conditions to return to normal once it passed.

The uptick in Chinese purchases suggests demand ahead of the northern winter is outweighing price concerns. items.summary: Oman’s Asyad Group has priced an institutional share sale in its listed shipping subsidiary at OMR50.8m ($132m), reducing its ownership as part of a move to broaden the company’s shareholder base. The transaction covers 5% of Asyad Shipping’s issued share capital. Upon completion, the company’s free float will rise to 25%, meeting the minimum requirement set by Oman’s Financial Services Authority. No new shares are being issued, and Asyad Shipping will not receive any of the funds. The group is also preparing a separate retail offering of up to 1.25% of the shipping company at the same price, subject to regulatory approval. The remaining shares held by Asyad Group will be subject to a 180-day lock-up following settlement. The transaction follows Asyad Shipping’s March 2025 initial public offering, which raised approximately $333m and brought 20% of the company into public ownership. Asyad operated a fleet of 91 vessels at the end of June, including 48 owned or co-owned ships, 31 chartered-in vessels and 12 newbuildings. items.title: Zijin Mining orders bulker pair for African mineral trade
items.original_title: Zijin Mining orders bulker pair for African mineral trade
items.summary: Chinese mining giant Zijin Mining has returned to Shandong Xinneng Shipbuilding for two 3,000 dwt bulk carriers, expanding its dedicated mineral transport operation on Lake Tanganyika in eastern Africa. The latest contract follows an earlier order for four 2,000 dwt vessels at the same Chinese yard, which are now operating on the lake between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Tanzania. The new ships will be 50% larger than their predecessors, adding a combined 6,000 dwt to Zijin’s lake transport capacity. Contract value and delivery dates have not been disclosed. The investment forms part of Zijin’s efforts to establish an alternative export corridor for minerals from its operations in the DRC. The group’s existing shipping operation links Congolese cargoes with Kigoma in Tanzania, from where they can move towards the country’s Indian Ocean export infrastructure. Zijin’s first four lake bulkers were built through an arrangement that saw hull sections manufactured in China and assembled in Tanzania, overcoming the logistical challenges of building vessels for an African inland waterway. The company established the route to support its growing mining interests in central Africa and reduce dependence on existing overland transport connections.
